title: Toem 2 Hands-On: A Delightful Photography Sim That Turns Errands into Joy
summary: Video game tourism usually means gawking at realistic landmarks, but Toem 2 captures something rarer: the actual feeling of being a tourist. In a recent hands-on demo, I wandered through Deltburg, a cozy riverside town with a plumbing problem, and discovered a sequel that makes even sewage issues feel like a pleasant detour. The demo dropped me into a tutorial with a talking butterfly, then introduced Plum — a character who moves like Mr. Game & Watch and runs Plum's Plumbing. He's got a giant clog in a pipe (origins mercifully unexplained) causing water to spray everywhere. He can't plunge and turn the valve simultaneously, so he hands you a screwdriver that attaches to your camera. Yes, your camera becomes a Swiss army knife; no, we don't question it. Plum is one of Toem 2's new 'Friends,' characters who give you tools and open up fresh puzzles. The screwdriver tasks ranged from simple valve-turning to a final brain-teaser where I traced a tangled pipe network using perspective. But the magic lies in how un-task-like everything feels. You're never told to go to the aquarium's back room for a mandatory quest — it's assumed you'll naturally wander there while exploring. And until you do, there's plenty else: a scent-maker who analyzes disgusting smells through your photos, a robot comedian who forgot what bikes look like, a sleepy rooftop guy craving coffee. Everyone has a problem, and you solve it with curiosity and a camera. I found myself photographing a singing bass just because, or helping an aquarium scientist guess evolutionary chains by snapping fish. The journal tracks quests and creatures, but I wasn't chasing completion. I just wanted to soak in the supremely chill black-and-white vibes. Even the snake in the river was charming — and I don't say that lightly. Toem 2 is planned for Q3 2026 on Switch, PlayStation, Xbox, and PC. It's a pressure-free wander where the real reward is the journey, though earning a new hat doesn't hurt.
why_it_matters: Toem 2 shows that games don’t need violence or pressure to be fun — it celebrates noticing small, weird details, which might inspire you to explore your own world with a camera or a sketchbook.

background_read: The original Toem (released in 2021 by the small Swedish studio Something We Made) was a photography adventure that won a BAFTA Games Award for its charming black-and-white world.
Plum’s jerky movement is a nod to Mr. Game & Watch (a simple character from Nintendo’s early 1980s LCD handheld games), a retro style that adds to the game’s quirky feel.
Cozy games — like Animal Crossing, Unpacking, and Toem — have become hugely popular for their relaxing, pressure-free gameplay that focuses on exploration and creativity rather than competition.
In the first Toem, players solved puzzles by taking proud little photographs; the sequel expands on that idea by giving the camera attachments, turning it into a multi-tool.

perspectives.description: Fans of stress-free, creative games will adore it. The gentle puzzles, charming characters, and black-and-white art offer a warm escape that rewards curiosity over skill.
Players who prefer fast action or complex systems might find Toem 2 too slow and unambitious. With no fail-states or intense goals, it could feel like a tech demo stretched into a full game.
Toem 2 fits into a broader design trend of 'wholesome games' that prioritize relaxation and mental well-being — a reaction against hyper-competitive multiplayer titles and crunch culture.

If the full game delivers enough variety and surprises beyond the demo, the expanded tool system could set a new standard for photography puzzles. Success might encourage more developers to build games around observation rather than combat.
